Question: How do I choose olives for an olive tapenade?

If you can find them, go for olives that are packed in brine rather than oil, as this will give you a fresher taste and better texture. Question: How do you know if you’ve kneaded whole-wheat dough enough? Is it supposed to be rougher than white bread dough?
Old_Answer: If your dough has a high percentage of whole wheat, more than 25%, it will feel different from an all white wheat dough. The higher the percentage of whole whest, the less likely you are to be able to use a windowpane test. You just need to make the same dough enough times thst you know when it feels right. You should be able to stretch the dough without breaking it, even if it won't be as thin as the typical windowpane test. Some of the roughness of the bran can be eliminated by doing a preferment with the whole grsin flour and a bit more water than ypu would use in an ordinary preferment. This softens the bran, making it easier to develop a good gluten structure. You can also simply extend the initial autolyse with all the flour, agsin using slightly more water, since whole wheat absorbs more water than regular white flour.
Answer_with_writing_sample: Kneading whole-wheat dough can indeed feel a bit different than working with white bread dough, but that's perfectly normal. Whole-wheat flour contains more bran and germ, which can give the dough a rougher texture. When you've kneaded it enough, the dough should become smoother and more elastic, even if it doesn't reach the same level of smoothness as white bread dough. A good way to test if you've kneaded it sufficiently is to perform the "windowpane test." Take a small piece of dough and stretch it gently between your fingers. If it stretches into a thin, translucent membrane without tearing, you're in good shape. If it tears easily, it likely needs more kneading. Generally, whole-wheat dough requires a bit more time and effort to develop gluten, so don't be discouraged if it feels rough at first. Aim for about 10 to 15 minutes of kneading, and remember that hydration plays a key role too; whole-wheat flour absorbs more water, so you might need to adjust your liquid ingredients accordingly. If the dough feels too dry or crumbly, adding a little more water can help. Ultimately, trust your instincts and the feel of the dough; it should be soft and pliable but not sticky. With practice, you'll get a better sense of when it's just right!

Additionally, consider using a simple syrup to brush over the cooled cake layers before frosting. This syrup, made from equal parts sugar and water, can be flavored with vanilla or citrus zest for an extra kick. By using these techniques, you can ensure your homemade cake remains deliciously moist and enjoyable for days to come.

In case you want to make pancakes from scratch, here's the recipe I use. If you want fluffier pancakes, whip the egg whites to stiff peaks and fold them in after you've combined the other ingredients. This recipe serves three or four people, depending on how hungry they are.. 250 grams flour (2 cups acooped & leveled) 2 large eggs 480 ml buttermilk (2 US cups) 1 1/2 tsp baking powder 1 tsp vanilla extract or 1/4 tsp almond extract 2 tbsp melted butter 2 tbsp granulated sugar Pinch salt (leave out if using salted butter) Combine the dry ingredients in one bowl, and the wet in another. Add the dry to the wet and stir until just combined. If you whipped the egg whites, fold in the egg whites. Let rest 10-15 minutes and preheat your pan or griddle. Use very little butter on the pan for even browning. This is a very flexible recipe. You can add spices like nutmeg, cinnamon, or allspice, you can add orange or lemon zest, you can use different kinds of flour. Sometimes I use a combination of rye and buckwheat, which is tasty. If you use whole grain flours, you may need a little more liquid.
Answer_with_writing_sample: Dense pancakes can be a common issue, and there are several reasons why this might happen. One of the most frequent culprits is overmixing the batter. When you combine the wet and dry ingredients, it's important to mix just until everything is incorporated. If you overmix, you develop the gluten in the flour too much, leading to a tougher, denser pancake. Another factor could be the leavening agents. Make sure you're using fresh baking powder or baking soda, as these are what help your pancakes rise and become fluffy. If your leavening agents are old, they may not produce the necessary lift. Additionally, consider the ratio of wet to dry ingredients; too much flour can also lead to density. A good rule of thumb is to use slightly less flour than the recipe calls for, or to add a bit more liquid if the batter seems too thick. Lastly, letting the batter rest for about 5-10 minutes before cooking can help, as it allows the flour to hydrate and the gluten to relax. This can lead to a lighter texture. If you want to experiment, you can also try folding in whipped egg whites at the end for added fluffiness. This technique introduces air into the batter, which can make a noticeable difference in the final product. So, keep these tips in mind, and you should be well on your way to making light and fluffy pancakes!

Question: How can I make bread with rapid rising yeast? I found it to not work as well as regular yeast.
Old_Answer: Rapid rise yeast is designed for use in bread machines. Because it is formulated with enzymes to speed up the process, it doesn't work well for breads that need a second proof, or for recipes where you want a long, slow rise at lower temperatures. That's one of the best ways to develop flavor in lean doughs, but you can't use rapid rise yeast to do it. There is apparently a distinction between quick rise and rapid rise yeasts, and the SAF instant yeast, but exactly what it is, isn't clear. I do know that SAF red can be used for recipes with cold rises, while SAF gold is preferred for sweet doughs, which can be slower to rise. I use SAF Red for all my home baking, and it seems to work just as well as active dry yeast. And according to several articles I found, the active dry yeast, st least the Fleischman’s brand, no longer needs to he proofed separately, because the processing has improved over the years, resulting in fewer dead yeast cells in the encapsulation. My usual process, when I come up against a question like this, is to make side by side recipes, see what results I get, then decide which I like best. So I guess there will be a couple of yeast experiments in the near future.
Answer_with_writing_sample: Making bread with rapid rising yeast, also known as instant yeast, can be a bit different from using regular yeast, but it can yield excellent results if you adjust your approach slightly. First, it's important to note that rapid rising yeast is designed to work faster, so you can skip the proofing step that you would typically do with active dry yeast. Just mix it directly with your dry ingredients. To get the best rise, make sure your water is warm, around 120°F to 130°F (49°C to 54°C), as this temperature activates the yeast quickly. You can combine the yeast with flour, salt, and any other dry ingredients before adding the warm water and any fats like oil or butter. Knead the dough until it's smooth and elastic, which usually takes about 8-10 minutes by hand or 5-7 minutes in a stand mixer. After kneading, let the dough rise in a warm place until it doubles in size, which should take about 30-45 minutes. Keep in mind that the rising time may vary based on the temperature of your kitchen. Once it has risen, shape it into your desired form, let it rest for another short rise of about 10-15 minutes, and then bake it in a preheated oven. If you find that your bread isn't rising as much as you'd like, consider checking the freshness of your yeast, as expired yeast can lead to disappointing results. Happy baking!

Question: Is it okay to deglaze a cast iron skillet?
Old_Answer: Absolutely okay. Cast iron skillets develop wonderful fond when searing meat, and deglazing is how you get all that flavor off the pan. If you're worried about ruining the seasoning on the pan, just use a wooden spoon.
Answer_with_writing_sample: Yes, it is absolutely okay to deglaze a cast iron skillet, and in fact, it's a great technique to enhance the flavors of your dish. After you've seared meat or sautéed vegetables, you'll notice those delicious browned bits stuck to the bottom of the skillet. Those bits, known as fond, are packed with flavor and can be incorporated into your sauce or gravy. To deglaze, simply add a liquid—like broth, wine, or even water—while the skillet is still hot. Use a wooden spoon or spatula to scrape up the fond as the liquid simmers. This not only helps lift those tasty morsels but also creates a rich base for your sauce. Just be mindful of the temperature; if the skillet is too hot, the liquid can evaporate quickly, leaving you with little to work with. Additionally, while cast iron is durable, avoid using acidic liquids like vinegar or citrus juice too frequently, as they can strip the seasoning over time. If you maintain your skillet well, deglazing can be a fantastic way to make the most of your cooking and add depth to your meals. Just remember to re-season your skillet afterward if you notice any wear on the surface. Overall, deglazing is a simple yet effective method to elevate your cooking while keeping your cast iron in good shape.

Question: How do you keep your sourdough from being too dense?
Old_Answer: The things that make sourdough or any bread too dense are actually fairly simple. Bread rises well when the dough has a well developed gluten structure, enough hydration to allow full expansion during fermentation, proofing, and baking, surface tension that encourages the loaf to rise up instead of out, and enough time at all stages for the yeast to create CO2, as well as helping develop the gluten and improve flavor. A final method to improve the crumb of your sourdough is proper oven prep, or baking in a cloche or dutch oven. None of these things are complicated in themselves, but learning to recognize when you've done it right takes practice. The biggest problem bakers who are new to sourdough run into is time. Sourdough cultures work more slowly than commercial yeast. It can take hours for a fed sourdough to reach its maximum activity, and more hours for the dough to ferment. You need to cultivate patience, and learn to recognize when your culture is ready and active. Some people recommend a float test, where you drop a small piece of the culture into a bowl of water and see if it floats. I prefer feeding the culture in a straight sided glass container, so I can see when it has doubled. High hydration is another key to lighter, airier breads. Bakers define hydration as the percentage of water in the dough using the total weight of flour as 100%. So a dough made with 1000 grams of flour at 70% hydration would need 700 grams of water. A typical sourdough recipe would call for a 20% inoculation, or 200 grams of fed, active sourdough starter. Many sourdoughs, especially the popular no knead breads, use hydrations in the range of 75% - 80%. These high hydration doughs need some practice to work with, but they are key to those impressive open crumb sourdoughs everyone seems so enamored with these days. Time. Time is the key to proper fermentation and proofing. While bread made with commercial yeast can be fully fermented and ready for shaping in 60-90 minutes, sourdough takes more time. The starter in the picture above takes five hours to double after feeding, at 80°F. Longer in cold weather. The dough made with it takes the same time for a first rise, after three stretch and folds at 30 minute intervals. Then it gets shaped and popped in the fridge for an overnight rise. Basically, a two day process instead of an afternoon of baking. Another key to a good rise is the shaping of the loaf. Developing surface tension as you shape your bread ensures that it will rise well. There are a lot of ways to do this, and dozens of videos by professional and hobby bakers demonstrating their techniques. Once the dough has proofed and is ready to go into the oven, slashing is another way to control and improve the rise. The last thing to think about is baking. There are ways to prepare a home oven to get a better rise. Professional ovens inject steam during the baking process. Home bakers can imitate this in several ways. One is to put a pan of boiling water in the bottom of the oven to create steam, or to spray the sides of your oven with water, close it for 30 seconds, spray it again, then put the bread in to bake. A pizza stone or steel, properly preheated for at least 45 minutes for the stone and slightly less for the steel, provides direct heat on the bottom of the loaf. A simpler method is to bake your bread in a dutch oven or a ceramic cloche. This traps steam, which lets the crust stay moist longer, encouraging it to expand. Both dutch ovens and ceramic cloches need to be thoroughly preheated to do the job. I know. This is a long answer to a simple question. But if you take it one step at a time, you will end up with better bread.
